questions.question: What is the primary difference between HTTP and HTTPS?

options.text: HTTPS encrypts data in transit using TLS
HTTPS uses a different port and protocol entirely

questions.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS—the same protocol encrypted. It uses port 443 (vs 80) but the HTTP semantics are identical. TLS adds encryption, not compression or speed.

questions.question: During a TLS handshake, what does the server send to prove its identity?

options.text: Digital certificate signed by a Certificate Authority

questions.explanation: The server presents its certificate, signed by a trusted CA, containing its public key. The client verifies the certificate chain to establish trust before encrypted communication.

questions.question: Which attacks does HTTPS protect against? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: HTTPS/TLS provides confidentiality (prevents eavesdropping), authentication (prevents MITM), and integrity (prevents tampering). SQL injection is an application-layer vulnerability unrelated to transport security.

questions.question: A website shows a certificate warning. What could cause this? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Certificate is for a different domain
Certificate is self-signed (not from trusted CA)
Website is using HTTP instead of HTTPS

questions.explanation: Certificate warnings occur for expired, mismatched domain, or untrusted (self-signed) certificates. HTTP sites don't show certificate warnings—they simply lack the padlock icon.

questions.question: What is the purpose of HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)?

options.text: To force browsers to only use HTTPS for a domain

questions.explanation: HSTS tells browsers to always use HTTPS for a domain, preventing downgrade attacks where an attacker redirects users to HTTP. Once set, browsers refuse HTTP connections to that domain.

questions.question: TLS 1.3 improved upon TLS 1.2 in which ways? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Removed support for weak cipher suites

questions.explanation: TLS 1.3: faster handshake (1-RTT), removed weak ciphers (RC4, SHA-1, etc.), and 0-RTT resumption. HTTP/2 is independent of TLS version—it works with TLS 1.2 too.

questions.question: A load balancer terminates TLS and forwards unencrypted traffic to backend servers. What is this called?
questions.explanation: TLS termination (SSL offloading) decrypts traffic at the load balancer, reducing backend server load. Traffic between LB and backends is unencrypted (or re-encrypted for end-to-end).

questions.question: Why might an organization use a private Certificate Authority for internal services?

options.text: Public CAs don't support internal domains
To avoid certificate costs and enable internal-only trust

questions.explanation: Private CAs allow issuing certificates for internal domains without public CA costs or validation requirements. Internal clients trust the private CA; external clients wouldn't.

questions.question: True or False: HTTPS guarantees that the website content is safe and trustworthy.
questions.explanation: HTTPS only ensures encrypted, authenticated transport. A malicious site can have valid HTTPS. It protects data in transit but says nothing about the site's content or intentions.

questions.question: What is certificate pinning?

options.text: Storing certificates on a physical device
Hardcoding expected certificates/keys in an application

questions.explanation: Certificate pinning embeds expected certificate or public key hashes in the application, rejecting connections even with valid CA-signed certificates if they don't match. Prevents CA compromise attacks.

questions.question: A company wants to inspect HTTPS traffic for security monitoring. What technique is required?

options.text: TLS interception with proxy and trusted CA

questions.explanation: HTTPS inspection requires a proxy that terminates TLS, inspects content, and re-encrypts. Clients must trust the proxy's CA. This is essentially an authorized MITM for security purposes.

questions.question: Which HTTP header helps prevent mixed content issues when migrating to HTTPS?
questions.explanation: CSP's upgrade-insecure-requests directive tells browsers to automatically upgrade HTTP resource requests to HTTPS, helping during migration when some resources still reference HTTP URLs.
